title: Behavioural: STAR and the Amazon Leadership Principles
seriesDescription: STAR stories, Amazon Leadership Principles, strong and weak answers. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Structure STAR answers, map situations to the 16 Amazon Leadership Principles, recall what each principle means and spot what strengthens or weakens a story.
source: Amazon Leadership Principles (aboutamazon.com); Amazon interview guide (aboutamazon.com) on STAR; Harvard Business Review on behavioural interviews; third-party prep guides for Bar Raiser details

questions.prompt: How many Amazon Leadership Principles are there today?
questions.explanation: There are 16. The two most recent additions (2021) are "Strive to be Earth's Best Employer" and "Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility".

questions.prompt: In 2021 Amazon extended its Leadership Principles from 14 to 16. How many principles were added?
questions.explanation: Two were added: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer, and Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility. The older 14 (Customer Obsession through Deliver Results) are what most technical stories map to.

questions.prompt: In your Result you say p95 latency fell from 800 ms to 200 ms. By what percentage did it fall?
questions.explanation: (800 - 200) / 800 = 75%. A number with a clear baseline is far more convincing than "much faster".

questions.prompt: Match each short story to the Leadership Principle it demonstrates best.

left.text: Fixed a flaky alert that no team owned because it kept paging customers
Read raw logs and found the dashboard double-counted retries
Disagreed with a design in review, then fully supported the team's decision
Replaced a three-service workflow with one scheduled job
Shipped a one-week prototype to test a reversible assumption

questions.explanation: Most stories fit two or three principles; lead with the one the question asks about and keep the others in reserve for follow-ups.

questions.prompt: Match each Leadership Principle to what it means.

right.text: Accomplish more with less; constraints breed resourcefulness
Listen attentively, speak candidly and be self-critical
Continually raise the bar and drive defect-free work
Create and communicate a bold direction that inspires results
Never done learning; always exploring ways to improve
Speed matters and many decisions are reversible

questions.explanation: The unused meaning belongs to Bias for Action. Know each principle in one plain sentence.

questions.text: STAR stands for {1}, Task, {2} and {3}; the {2} section should carry most of the answer because it shows what you personally did.
questions.explanation: Keep Situation and Task short, spend your time on Action, and finish with a measurable Result and what you learned.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In a STAR answer most of the time should be spent on the Action.
questions.reason: Interviewers are assessing your individual contribution, not the team's overall outcome.

whys.a: Correct: Action is where your decisions, trade-offs and ownership are visible.

questions.explanation: Say "I" for your own actions and name teammates briefly when they contributed.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Saying only "we" throughout a story hides your own contribution.
questions.reason: Interviewers want to hear only about solo projects, never about teamwork.

whys.a: R is false so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not just unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true, but R is false; teamwork stories are welcome as long as your role is explicit.

questions.explanation: A good test: could someone write down what you did, step by step, from your answer?

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Disagree and Commit means you keep resisting a decision after it has been made until you are proven right.
questions.reason: Once a decision is made, leaders support it fully even if they argued against it earlier.

whys.b: A is false, so the pair cannot be both-true.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false and R is true. You voice disagreement before the decision, then commit wholeheartedly.

questions.explanation: Strong stories show the data you brought, the respectful push-back, and how you executed the final decision.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Where possible, a story's Result should include a measurable outcome.
questions.reason: A single strong story can often be reused for more than one Leadership Principle.

whys.a: R is true but about reuse, not about measuring results.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true and independent.

questions.explanation: Prepare roughly 8 to 10 stories with numbers, each tagged with two or three principles.

questions.prompt: Which sentence most weakens a STAR story that is meant to show Ownership?

options.text: "That part was the platform team's job, so I flagged it and moved on."
options.why: Right: Ownership means acting beyond your narrow remit when it serves the customer.

options.text: "I took over the runbook after the incident, although it was never assigned to me, and fixed the gaps."
options.why: This strengthens the story by showing initiative.

options.text: "I measured the problem first, then decided on the fix with the owning team's agreement."
options.why: Data plus collaboration strengthens ownership.

options.text: "I stayed until the alerts stayed green for a week and wrote down what I learned."
options.why: Follow-through is a sign of ownership.

questions.explanation: Interviewers listen for scope: did you act on things nobody asked you to, and see them through?

questions.prompt: Asked "Tell me about a time you failed", which answer is strongest?

options.text: A real mistake you caused, its impact, what you changed, and how it has not recurred.
options.why: Right: ownership, honesty and learning with evidence.

options.text: A failure that was really the fault of a colleague who missed the specification.
options.why: Blaming others signals low ownership.

options.text: "I cannot think of a failure because I always double-check everything before releasing it."
options.why: This reads as lacking self-awareness or being evasive.

options.text: "I sometimes work too hard and care too much, and that has occasionally slowed me down."
options.why: A disguised strength is a well-known non-answer.

questions.explanation: Choose a real, moderate-stakes failure, and finish with a systemic fix (a test, a checklist, an alert), not just "I will try harder".

questions.prompt: Which of these is an Amazon Leadership Principle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Frugality
options.why: Right: accomplish more with less.

options.text: Dive Deep
options.why: Right: stay close to the details and audit often.

options.text: Bias for Action
options.why: Right: speed matters in business.

options.text: Move Fast and Break Things
options.why: This is a slogan associated with Facebook, not an Amazon principle.

questions.explanation: Be careful with look-alikes from other companies' values.

questions.prompt: Write one or two sentences for the Result part of a STAR story about reducing API latency. Include a number with a before-and-after comparison, and say what you changed so it would not regress.
questions.model: Result: p95 latency fell from 800 ms to 200 ms (75%), timeouts dropped from 40 a day to 2, and I added a load test to CI so the regression would be caught before release.
questions.explanation: This free-text question is graded by simple keyword patterns; any answer with a measured change and a preventive step passes. Quantify with a baseline.

questions.prompt: In an Amazon-style interview loop, what is the Bar Raiser?

options.text: A specially trained interviewer from outside the hiring team who helps keep the hiring bar high.
options.why: Right: independence from the team is the point, and the Bar Raiser's view carries special weight in the debrief.

options.text: The hiring manager's own manager, who signs the offer letter after the loop has finished.
options.why: The role is an independent interviewer, not a place in the reporting chain.

options.text: A recruiter who negotiates the salary and the start date once the candidate has accepted.
options.why: Compensation is handled by recruiting, not by the Bar Raiser.

options.text: A coding judge who grades only the algorithm round and does not ask behavioural questions.
options.why: Bar Raisers also probe Leadership Principles, so prepare stories for them as well.

questions.explanation: Third-party prep guides describe a trained interviewer from another team with a strong say, often described as a veto, in the debrief; Amazon does not publish the details, so treat specifics as folklore. Practical takeaway: expect deep follow-ups on every story.

questions.prompt: Which of these were added to the Leadership Principles in the 2021 update from 14 to 16? Select all that apply.

options.text: Strive to be Earth's Best Employer
options.why: One of the two additions announced in 2021.

options.text: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility
options.why: The other 2021 addition, about the company's wider impact.

options.text: Learn and Be Curious
options.why: Added earlier (around 2015), so it was not part of the 2021 update.

options.text: Deliver Results
options.why: One of the original principles, not a 2021 addition.

questions.explanation: Know the two newest by name; interviewers rarely ask about them directly, but 'Earth's Best Employer' stories (mentoring, safety, inclusion) are increasingly common.
